text:
This section examines Experiment I —
Sparse n=7 parity boundary

from first principles. Keep two questions
separate: does changing the

order change the measured outcome, and
does the proposed search

method beat a matched alternative at the
same distinct-evaluation budget?

Search space: all 5,040 orderings
enumerated. Optimum: 1.0000 held by

14 orderings, only 0.28%; landscape
standard deviation 0.113. Historical

default: population 20 and mutation
probability 0.05; only 4/15 seeds

hit an optimum after roughly 103 distinct
evaluations. Random comparison:

at that same approximate budget, random’s
expected success was about

31%, close to prism’s 27%. Tuned prism:
population 40, mutation

0.6; 15/15 hits at about 384 mean
evaluations. Random: about

318 mean evaluations in the recorded
comparison. 40-seed audit: elitist

prism 19/40 hits, random 30/40; Wilson
intervals overlapped. Conclusion:

evolution had no reliable advantage on
this near-zero-locality landscape.

The correct action is random sampling or a
better representation.

Visual: display the apparent “15 out of
15” win, then

normalize by distinct evaluation cost and
reveal that random is

at least as competitive. Now read evidence
panel I-audit. The

axes, units, and sample are stated on
screen. The sample

represented here is all 5,040 orderings.
Raw observations remain visible

wherever the artifact provides them.
Censored observations stay marked at

the cap rather than becoming invented
hitting times, and sampled

landscapes leave unobserved permutations
blank. The supported finding is:

Conclusion: evolution had no reliable
advantage on this near-zero-locality

landscape. The broader claim not
established here is: Optimum: 1.0000

held by 14 orderings, only 0.28%;
landscape standard deviation 0.113.

This evidence changed the program as
follows: Carry this constraint

into the next experiment and compare
methods at equal cost.

The distinction is part of the result. A
large ordering

effect does not automatically imply an
evolutionary-search advantage, and

almost-sure convergence does not promise
practical efficiency.
